nodes.label: Armenia after Alexander
nodes.full: At the partition of Babylon in 323 BC Armenia was given to Neoptolemus, but he was beaten by Eumenes within a year and the land reverted to local satraps of the Orontid house. Diodorus names the Armenian satrap in 316 BC as Orontes, in some texts Ardoates, in the service of Antigonus.
nodes.src: Diodorus 18.3.1, 18.29, 19.23.3; Plutarch, Eumenes 4; Robert Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001).

nodes.label: Orontid kingdom
nodes.full: In the third century the Orontids ruled Armenia from Armavir, in the Araxes plain, as vassal kings under Seleucid overlordship, with an aristocracy of Iranian and local houses. Greek inscriptions of the third and second centuries at Armavir show a court that used Greek for its documents.
nodes.src: Armavir Greek inscriptions (Armavir excavations); Hewsen 2001; Nina Garsoïan in R. Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People, vol. 1 (1997).

nodes.label: Xerxes of Arsamosata
nodes.full: Xerxes, an Orontid king of Sophene and Armenia, whose seat was Arsamosata on the upper Euphrates, was besieged by Antiochus III in 212 BC; he came to terms, paid tribute and received the king's sister Antiochis as wife, and was left in his kingdom. He is the last Orontid to appear in the sources.

nodes.label: Artaxias I
nodes.full: After the Seleucid defeat at Magnesia in 190 BC two of Antiochus III's generals, Artaxias in Armenia and Zariadris in Sophene, declared themselves kings, and Strabo notes that they enlarged their lands at the expense of neighbours. Artaxias founded Artaxata (Artashat) on the Araxes as his capital and gave his name to a dynasty which ruled to AD 12.

nodes.label: Artavasdes I and Tigranes I
nodes.full: The successors of Artaxias, Artavasdes I and Tigranes I, held the kingdom through a century of Seleucid decay and Parthian pressure. Their reigns are poorly documented, known mainly from later Armenian tradition and a few remarks of Greek writers, and mark a period of growing Parthian pressure on the eastern marches.

nodes.label: Tigranes the Great
nodes.full: Tigranes II extended Armenia from the Caucasus to Syria and Cappadocia, took the title 'King of Kings' and the diadem and tiara of the Great King, and founded a new capital, Tigranocerta, to hold his empire. He was defeated by Lucullus in 69 BC and submitted to Pompey in 66, keeping only Armenia proper, as a Roman client.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Lucullus 21–36, Pompey 33; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 67, 104; Hewsen 2001.

nodes.label: Artavasdes II
nodes.full: The son of Tigranes allied with Rome and then Parthia, advised Crassus in 53 BC and was drawn into Antony's failed Median campaign of 36 BC. Antony then lured him to a parley, and took him in chains to Alexandria, where he was paraded in Antony's triumph in 34 BC and was executed after Actium, in 31 or 30. He wrote tragedies and histories in Greek.

nodes.label: Artaxias II and Tigranes III
nodes.full: Artaxias II came to the throne with Parthian help in 34 BC and was murdered about 20 BC; the Roman Tiberius then installed his brother Tigranes III. Armenia became a field between Rome and Parthia with kings from the dynasty set up by one or the other, a pattern which continued down to the first century AD.

nodes.label: Pharnavaz I
nodes.full: Georgian chronicles of the eleventh century recount that Pharnavaz, a local noble, freed Kartli ('Iberia' to the Greeks) from the governor appointed by Alexander and founded the first kingdom, with its capital at Mtskheta and the fortress Armaztsikhe on the Kura. The story is a medieval construct from older traditions; archaeology confirms an Iberian state at Mtskheta by the third century BC.
nodes.src: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Leonti Mroveli, The Life of the Kings); Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963); Mtskheta excavations.

nodes.label: Pharnavazid kings
nodes.full: The Georgian chronicles list as successors of Pharnavaz the kings Saurmag, Mirvan, Artaxias, Artag and Pharnajom; the Greek writers know the Iberian king only from 65 BC, when Pompey's invasion forced the king Artoces to submit. The Iberians were an agricultural lowland people with a warlike mountain periphery.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Pompey 34; Strabo 11.3; Toumanoff 1963; Rapp, Georgian Christian Identity (2003).

nodes.label: Pontic Colchis
nodes.full: Mithridates VI of Pontus subjected Colchis in the late second century BC, and governed it by his son Mithridates Chrestus and then through 'sceptre-bearers', local governors who changed often. Strabo describes the Colchians as the king's subjects with a large share in his armies and fleet, and the land as the last refuge of the king in 66 BC.
nodes.src: Strabo 11.2.18; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 15, 64, 101; Lordkipanidze, Archäologie in Georgien (1991).

nodes.label: Atropatene
nodes.full: North-west Media, ruled from the time of Alexander by Atropates and his descendants, kept its independence from the Seleucids; its king Artabazanes, who resisted Antiochus III in 220 BC, gave in only to a large army. The dynasty ruled as a Median-Iranian kingdom to the Parthian period.

nodes.label: Kingdom of Albania
nodes.full: The Albanians, the people between the lower Kura and the Caspian, formed a kingdom of many tribes under a king, whom Strabo says ruled over 26 languages; its king in 65 BC was Oroezes, who fought Pompey's army beside the Kura with his brother Cosis. The kingdom's capital was at Kabalaka (Gabala) in later sources.

nodes.label: Antiochus III in Armenia
nodes.full: Antiochus III marched into Armenia in 212 BC and besieged Xerxes in Arsamosata, a strong place on the Euphrates; the king capitulated, was confirmed on his throne with a marriage and agreed to pay arrears of tribute. The campaign restored Seleucid overlordship over Armenia and Sophene.

nodes.label: Armenian generals break away
nodes.full: After Antiochus III was beaten by Rome at Magnesia in 190 BC, his strategoi of Armenia and Sophene, Artaxias and Zariadris, took advantage of his defeat to proclaim themselves kings, with Roman toleration. The Seleucid hold on the highlands ended there, though Antiochus IV later campaigned against Artaxias.

nodes.label: Conquests of Tigranes
nodes.full: Tigranes II took the Parthian territories of northern Mesopotamia and Media, intervened in Cappadocia, and in 83 BC accepted the throne of Syria from the factions of the Seleucid kingdom, reigning from Antioch for fourteen years. Armenia's empire covered a swathe from the Caspian to the Mediterranean and was the greatest in the East between the Seleucids and the Romans.
nodes.src: Appian, Syrian Wars 48, Mithridatic Wars 67; Justin 40.1–2; Strabo 11.14.15.

nodes.label: Tigranocerta
nodes.full: On 6 October 69 BC the Roman general Lucullus, with a small army of perhaps 12,000 to 15,000 men, defeated a much larger Armenian army under Tigranes outside his new city of Tigranocerta and took the city and its treasure; in 68 he marched on Artaxata, but his troops mutinied. The victory ended Tigranes's empire in Syria.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Lucullus 25–32; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 84–87; Dio 35.

nodes.label: Pompey in the Caucasus
nodes.full: In 66 BC Pompey took over from Lucullus, pursued Mithridates VI to the Caucasus, accepted Tigranes's surrender in the Armenian camp, and in 65 invaded the Iberian and Albanian lands, defeating Artoces and Oroezes on the Kura, and marched to the Phasis in Colchis. It is the first Roman army in the Caucasus.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Pompey 32–38; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 103; Dio 36.45–37.5.

nodes.label: Carrhae
nodes.full: In 53 BC Artavasdes II offered Crassus an army if he would invade Parthia by way of Armenia's hills; Crassus took the desert road instead, and was crushed at Carrhae. Plutarch has the head of Crassus brought to the royal wedding at Artaxata as the actors performed Euripides' Bacchae.

nodes.label: Antony and Artavasdes
nodes.full: Antony marched through Armenia in 36 BC against Atropatene and the Parthians; Artavasdes withdrew his cavalry in the course of the campaign and the army returned shattered. In 34 Antony invaded Armenia, captured the king and annexed it briefly, with his son Alexander Helios named King of Armenia in the Donations of Alexandria.

nodes.label: Boundary stones of Artaxias
nodes.full: A group of stones inscribed in Aramaic with the name of King Artaxias, found around Lake Sevan and in Zangezur and elsewhere in the highlands, mark the limits of royal domains and estates. They show a king with an administration, a land survey, and Aramaic as its language, and echo Armenian tradition that Artashes surveyed the land.
nodes.src: Artashes Aramaic boundary stones (Sevan, Zangezur); Movses Khorenatsi 2.5; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Settlement with Pompey
nodes.full: In 66 BC Tigranes came to Pompey's camp, laid his diadem at the general's feet and was returned the kingdom of Armenia itself, as a friend and ally of Rome, though he lost Syria, Cappadocia and his other conquests and had to pay a heavy indemnity, reported as 6,000 talents. Armenia became a client state.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Pompey 33; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 104–105; Dio 36.53.

nodes.label: Four orders of Iberia
nodes.full: Strabo reports for Iberia four classes: the first, from which the king was chosen, the second the priests who handled justice and borders, the third the soldiers and farmers, and the fourth the common people, who were the king's slaves, and the king ruled over all. The description gives an early view of a Caucasian social order.

nodes.label: Eristavi
nodes.full: The Georgian chronicles attribute to Pharnavaz the division of the kingdom into districts governed by eristavi, 'leaders of the people', under a chief minister, the spaspet, an organisation which later Georgian kings continued. Whether the system dates to the third century BC cannot be proved.
nodes.src: Leonti Mroveli, The Life of the Kings; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Anahit and the golden statue
nodes.full: The Armenians gave great honours to Anahit, the Iranian goddess of waters, identified with the Greek Artemis, whose rich temple at Erez in Acilisene held a golden statue; Pliny relates that in the time of Antony a soldier plundered it and became so rich that he entertained Augustus. The temple was the greatest of the Armenian cult places.

nodes.label: Albanian moon cult
nodes.full: Strabo writes that the Albanians worshipped Zeus, the Sun and the Moon, above all the Moon, whose temple lay near Iberia and whose priest, second in rank to the king, controlled a sacred estate and its temple servants, some of whom, inspired, prophesied. A man chosen by the god was sacrificed to the Moon.

nodes.label: Idols of Mtskheta
nodes.full: The Georgian chronicles describe Pharnavaz setting on a hill above the Kura at Armaztsikhe the idol of the chief god Armazi, a bronze man in armour with sword and eyes of precious stones, and idols of the gods Gatsi and Gaim, later joined by Zaden. Mtskheta remained the national shrine until the conversion.

nodes.label: Coins of Tigranes
nodes.full: Tigranes struck silver tetradrachms at Antioch, with his head in the tall tiara with an eagle and star, and on the back the Tyche of Antioch with the river god Orontes, in the Seleucid fashion. The royal portrait in Persian dress and the Greek legend 'of King of Kings Tigranes' show the court's two worlds.

nodes.label: Theatre of Tigranocerta
nodes.full: Tigranes filled his new capital with deportees and wealth and gave it a theatre, built for the performance of Greek plays; Plutarch says that the Greek actors collected for its opening were seized by Lucullus and used for his own victory games. The king's court included Greek rhetoricians and historians such as Amphicrates.

nodes.label: Artavasdes’s tragedies
nodes.full: Artavasdes II composed tragedies, speeches and histories in Greek, none of which survives, and Plutarch notes that the king and Orodes of Parthia were watching a performance of Euripides' Bacchae when the head of Crassus was brought in. The court was Hellenised in language and culture.

nodes.label: Greek inscriptions of Armavir
nodes.full: Some twenty Greek inscriptions of the third and second centuries BC found at Armavir, on the hill of the former Urartian Argishtihinili, include dedications and administrative texts, and show that Greek was used at the court and in the town. They are the oldest historical documents in Armenian soil after the Urartian.
nodes.src: Armavir Greek inscriptions (Armenian Academy of Sciences); Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Vani under the Pontic kings
nodes.full: The hill-town of Vani continued to flourish in the Hellenistic period, with its terraced sanctuary, houses with tiled roofs, Greek inscriptions and rich burials of gold, silver and bronze; it was destroyed by fire in the first century BC, probably in the time of Mithridates's wars. The site has produced the finest Hellenistic objects of the Caucasus.

nodes.label: Hannibal at Artaxata
nodes.full: Strabo and Plutarch relate that Hannibal, an exile at the court of Antiochus III and then of Artaxias, told the Armenian king of the good site at the bend of the Araxes and designed the new city of Artaxata. The tradition is of the sort that attached famous names to famous cities, and cannot be verified.

nodes.label: Aramaic and Greek
nodes.full: The Armenian kings used Aramaic for administration and boundaries, as the stones of Artaxias show, and Greek for royal correspondence, coinage and literature, as the Armavir inscriptions and Artavasdes show, while the people spoke Armenian, which was not written until the fifth century AD. The court's languages were thus those of its Iranian and Greek neighbours.
nodes.src: Artashes boundary stones; Armavir Greek inscriptions; Garsoïan 1997.

nodes.label: Strabo on the Caucasus
nodes.full: Strabo, born at Amasya, devoted the eleventh book of his Geography to the Caucasian lands, Iberia, Albania, Colchis and Armenia, drawing on earlier historians of Pompey's and Mithridates's wars, such as Theophanes of Mytilene. It is the chief literary description of the region for the period.

nodes.label: Georgian Chronicles
nodes.full: The royal narrative of the Georgian lands, called Kartlis Tskhovreba, with its first part, the 'Life of the Kings' by Leonti Mroveli of about the eleventh century, supplies the names and order of the Iberian kings but was compiled more than a thousand years after the events from older oral and written tradition, and its chronology cannot be relied on without confirmation from outside sources.

nodes.label: Trade routes of Armenia
nodes.full: Armenia lay across the roads from the Black Sea and the Caucasus to Mesopotamia and Syria, from the Phasis and Kura to the Euphrates; Strabo calls Artaxata the royal seat of Armenia, built on a peninsula of the Araxes, and the roads gave the cities along them a share in the traffic.

nodes.label: Plains and raiders
nodes.full: Strabo describes the plain of Iberia, the Kura valley, as a rich country with farms, towns and roofs of tile in the Greek fashion, and the Armenian plain of the Araxes as fertile too, producing grain, vine, fruit and the horses of Armenia and Media. The mountains behind were the home of herders and bandits.

nodes.label: Artaxata and Tigranocerta
nodes.full: Artaxias founded Artaxata, c. 176 BC, on a loop of the Araxes, with the Khor Virap hill as its citadel, and Tigranes built Tigranocerta, 'the city of Tigranes', with a palace, parks, hunting grounds and strong walls. The two capitals were laid out on the model of Hellenistic royal cities.
nodes.src: Strabo 11.14.6; Plutarch, Lucullus 26; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 84; Artaxata excavations (Khachatryan).

nodes.label: Problem of Tigranocerta
nodes.full: The exact site of Tigranes's capital, taken by the Romans in 69 BC and again by Corbulo in AD 59, has never been securely identified. Candidates include Silvan (Martyropolis), Arzan and Tell Ermen, near Batman and Diyarbakır in modern Turkey; scholars rely on Plutarch's and Tacitus's accounts of the Roman marches and the topography. The question remains unresolved.
nodes.src: Plutarch, Lucullus 25–28; Tacitus, Annals 15.4–5; Hewsen 2001 on the site debate.

nodes.label: Deported cities
nodes.full: To populate Tigranocerta Tigranes deported thousands of people from Cappadocia, Cilicia, Syria and Arabian tribes, together with the Greek craftsmen and actors of cities of the former Seleucid land, and gave the new capital a cosmopolitan population. When the Romans took the city, most of them returned to their homes.
nodes.src: Strabo 12.2.9; Plutarch, Lucullus 21, 26, 29; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 67.

nodes.label: Alliance of Pontus and Armenia
nodes.full: Mithridates VI of Pontus gave his daughter Cleopatra in marriage to Tigranes, and the two kings coordinated their conquests, Tigranes taking Cappadocia for Mithridates while Mithridates held the Pontic and Colchian lands. When the Roman attack came, Tigranes at first hesitated to take his father-in-law into his kingdom.
nodes.src: Justin 38.3; Appian, Mithridatic Wars 15, 67; Plutarch, Lucullus 14.

nodes.label: Seventy valleys
nodes.full: Strabo tells that Tigranes, while a hostage in Parthia, paid for his release with the cession of seventy valleys in Armenia to the Parthian king, which he took back when he became king and defeated the Parthians. It marks the early rivalry of Armenia and Parthia over the border lands of Atropatene and Media.

nodes.label: From Seleucid satrapy to Roman client
nodes.full: In the three centuries after Alexander the Caucasus passed from the Persian empire to successor kingdoms, to local dynasties and finally under the influence of Rome and Parthia. By 1 BC Armenia, Iberia and Albania were client or neighbouring kingdoms of the Roman frontier, drawn into the politics of the two empires.

nodes.label: Shepherds of Albania
nodes.full: Strabo says that the Albanians, tall and handsome, were mostly herders and fought on foot and horse with bow and javelin, that they had no knowledge of accurate weights and measures and would not count above a hundred, and that they used barter rather than coin. His account is second-hand, from Pompey's officers.

nodes.label: Antiochis and Cleopatra
nodes.full: Two royal women of the Seleucid and Pontic houses were married into Armenia: Antiochis, sister of Antiochus III, who was given to Xerxes of Arsamosata in 211 BC as the pledge of peace, and Cleopatra, daughter of Mithridates VI, who became the queen of Tigranes about 94 BC. Both were instruments of diplomacy, and little is known of their lives.

nodes.label: Gaugamela and Mithrenes
nodes.full: At Gaugamela on 1 October 331 BC the Armenians fought under Orontes and Mithraustes, and Alexander afterwards gave the satrapy to Mithrenes.
